**Holding.** No. The power to recognize foreign states and governments belongs to the President alone, and Sec. 214(d) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, which required the listing, unconstitutionally infringed it.

**Question.** Whether Congress could require the State Department, on request, to list "Israel" as the place of birth in the passports of U.S. citizens born in Jerusalem, contrary to the executive's policy of not recognizing any state's sovereignty over the city.

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Zivotofsky v. Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zivotofsky_v._Kerry) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

The Court upheld the President's refusal to follow a foreign affairs statute, finding the power exclusive even in the third, "lowest ebb" category of [Jackson's framework](../cases/youngstown-1952.qmd); the Chief Justice's dissent called it the first time the Court had accepted "a President's direct defiance of an Act of Congress in the field of foreign affairs." At the same time it declined to treat [Curtiss-Wright](../cases/curtiss-wright-1936.qmd)'s "sole organ" language as making the President's foreign affairs power exclusive in general, and it stressed Congress's many powers in the field.

## Status

Good law.

## Statutes at issue

- [Constitution (war powers)](../statutes/constitution-war-powers.qmd){.subj}. Held the recognition power is exclusively the President's, and rejected a general reading of Curtiss-Wright's 'sole organ' language.

Studied in [Unit 1: Where the power comes from](../study/units/foundations.qmd).
